title: The recovery secret of a champion
passage: Three-time national sprint champion Dez Calloway wears Magnara copper bands every single day. 'They've completely changed my recovery,' he says. If they work for one of the fastest men alive, imagine what they'll do for your sore knees. Two bands for $39, free shipping this week only.
cue: If they work for one of the fastest men alive
explanation: The ad treats a sprinter's endorsement as proof that copper bands relieve joint pain. Dez knows sprinting, not medicine, and the ad offers no evidence that the bands do anything.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The ad leans on one famous athlete's word, not on how many people use the bands.

passage:
Grandpa Tunde: Don't install the phone update tonight. My friend Lionel says updates are how they secretly slow down older phones.
Femi: Lionel... your dentist?
Grandpa Tunde: He's a doctor, Femi. A very smart man. If he says it, I trust it.
cue: He's a doctor, Femi. A very smart man. If he says it, I trust it.
explanation: Grandpa trusts Lionel on phone software because he's a respected dentist. Dental training says nothing about how phone updates work.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Grandpa relies on one person's status, not on how many people believe the claim.

title: Thoughts after curriculum night
passage: Hi Ms. Duarte, thank you for a great curriculum night. I loved the focus on word problems, and the new homework portal is much easier to use. One concern: bestselling novelist Corinne Hale, whose kids attend Westbrook, has written that this discovery-based math leaves children confused. She's a brilliant thinker, and I'd like the school to reconsider.
cue: She's a brilliant thinker, and I'd like the school to reconsider.
explanation: Renata asks the school to rethink its math approach because a famous novelist criticized it. Corinne's talent as a writer doesn't make her an authority on how children learn math.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Renata cites one celebrated person, not a crowd; the trouble is that the novelist's expertise lies elsewhere.

passage: Day 12 of cold plunges after my morning lift. The first minute is brutal, I won't lie, and my towel budget has doubled. Grandmaster Viktor Sandor, one of the greatest chess minds alive, does it every morning and says cold water 'resets your immune system.' If a mind like that swears by it, that's good enough for me.
cue: If a mind like that swears by it, that's good enough for me.
explanation: Nadia accepts a health claim because a chess champion makes it. Brilliance at chess isn't expertise in immunology, and no evidence is offered for the 'reset'.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Nadia relies on a single admired figure, not on the popularity of cold plunges.

source: Board chair Leonard Fitch · Halverton school board
passage: We've heard a lot tonight about sleep studies supporting a later start, and I've read some of them. But I'd remind everyone that Dr. Anjali Rao, a cardiologist who has practiced in this county for thirty years, told us last month that a 45-minute shift makes no real difference to teenagers' health. If anyone understands health, it's her. I'm comfortable keeping our schedule.
cue: If anyone understands health, it's her.
explanation: Leonard sets the sleep research aside in favor of one respected doctor's opinion. Dr. Rao is a heart specialist, not a sleep researcher, and her view runs against the studies he just mentioned.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: Leonard isn't judging the sleep studies by their origin; he overrides them with one doctor's standing outside her specialty.

title: Analysts raise battery outlook after Kaplan's bold forecast
passage: Investor Sloane Kaplan, whose early bets on three software giants made her a billionaire, told a conference Thursday that new home batteries will halve household electricity bills within five years. Analysts at Grayfield Research accepted her claim about halving electricity bills the next morning, citing her unmatched record of spotting winners.
cue: citing her unmatched record of spotting winners
explanation: The analysts accept a prediction about electricity bills because a celebrated software investor made it. Her record picking software companies doesn't make her an expert on battery chemistry or energy costs.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The analysts aren't following a crowd; they defer to one investor's reputation in a field outside her expertise.

passage:
Camila: The crack in the basement wall is freaking me out. Do we need to reinforce the foundations?
Diego: Both the structural engineer we hired and the city inspector said it's shrinkage, not sinking foundations, and they wrote their reports separately. Two independent experts who looked at the actual wall agree, so no reinforcement needed.
Camila: Okay, I can breathe.
cue: Both the structural engineer we hired and the city inspector said it's shrinkage, not sinking foundations
explanation: Diego relies on two relevant experts who examined the actual crack and reached the same conclusion independently. That's exactly the kind of authority worth trusting.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: Both sources are experts in foundations, both inspected this wall, and they agree independently, so deferring to them is reasonable.

source: Parks director Wendell Ames · Kestrel Point council
passage: Three certified arborists, or tree specialists, have examined the Founders Oak, including one hired by the residents who want it saved. All three found extensive decay in the trunk. Their drill tests show less than a third of the wood is sound. When every expert, including one hired by its defenders, reaches the same verdict, we have to accept that the tree is at serious risk of falling.
cue: including one hired by the residents who want it saved
explanation: Wendell defers to arborists, the right experts, who all examined the tree and agree, including one with every reason to disagree. He also cites their measurements, not just their titles.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: These are relevant experts in agreement, backed by drill measurements, and one was hired by the other side, so the appeal is strong, not fallacious.
